text: Lotfi Aliasger Zadeh (/ˈzɑːdeɪ/; Azerbaijani: Lütfi Rəhim oğlu Ələsgərzadə; Persian: لطفی علی‌عسکرزاده; 4 February 1921 – 6 September 2017) was a mathematician, computer scientist, electrical engineer, artificial intelligence researcher, and professor of computer science at the University of California, Berkeley. He is best known for proposing fuzzy mathematics, which includes fuzzy sets, fuzzy logic, fuzzy algorithms, fuzzy semantics, fuzzy languages, fuzzy control, fuzzy systems, fuzzy probabilities, fuzzy events, and fuzzy information. Zadeh was a founding member of the Eurasian Academy. Born in Baku, Azerbaijan SSR, as Lotfi Aliasgerzadeh, he had an Iranian Muslim Azerbaijani father, Rahim Aleskerzade, a journalist from Ardabil, and a Jewish pediatrician mother, Fanya (Feyga) Korenman, from Odesa, Ukraine, who was an Iranian citizen. The family lived well in Baku due to the Soviet government's attraction of foreign correspondents, and Zadeh attended elementary school there for three years, which he said had a significant and long-lasting influence on his thinking. In 1931, when Stalin began agricultural collectivization and Zadeh was ten, his father moved the family to Tehran, Iran, where he attended Alborz High School, a missionary school, for eight years and met his future wife, Fay (Faina) Zadeh. She noted that the Presbyterian missionaries from the United States influenced her deeply, instilling in her a desire to live in the United States. During this time, Zadeh was awarded several patents. He placed third in the Iran national university exams and ranked first in his class in his first two years. In 1942, he graduated from the University of Tehran with a degree in electrical engineering, one of only three students in that field that year, due to World War II-related turmoil, when over 30,000 American soldiers were stationed in Iran, and Zadeh worked with his father, who conducted business with them as a contractor. In 1943, Zadeh decided to go to the United States for further education, traveling via Cairo after delays in obtaining proper papers and a suitable ship, arriving in mid-1944. He lived in New York, worked for an electronic association, and entered MIT as a graduate student in September 1944. While in the U.S., he shortened his family name, becoming Lotfi Aliasker Zadeh. He received his MS in electrical engineering from MIT in 1946. In 1947, after his parents settled in New York, he joined Columbia University as an engineer and was admitted as a doctoral student, receiving a PhD in electrical engineering in 1949 and becoming an assistant professor the following year. He taught at Columbia for ten years and was promoted to full professor in 1957. The chairman of the electronic engineering department at the University of California, Berkeley, offered him a position, and in 1959 he joined the university's electrical engineering faculty. During his research career, Zadeh made key contributions in linear system theory and classical control systems, and in fuzzy sets and fuzzy logic. In 1965, he published his seminal work on fuzzy sets, describing the motivation of replicating human-like reasoning and detailing the mathematics of fuzzy set theory. In 1973, he proposed his theory of fuzzy logic. Together, fuzzy sets and fuzzy logic provide foundations for innovations such as fuzzy control, fuzzy systems, and others. He was also on the Board of Governors for the International Neural Network Society (INNS) in 2003. In 1963, Zadeh became chair of the Department of Electrical Engineering at UC Berkeley and initiated the transformation of the department into the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) by 1968, a move that advanced UC Berkeley's standing in computer science and influenced other universities globally. He received the IEEE Education Award in 1973 for his leadership in EE and EECS. He served on various Academic Senate committees at UC Berkeley, including Academic Planning & Resource Allocation (1992–95), Committees (1969–70; 1980–81), Courses of Instruction (1975–80), and Faculty Awards (1990–92), and graduated over 50 PhD students, many of whom became leaders in engineering, management, and information sciences. Zadeh photographed people around him. He was described as "quick to shrug off nationalism," stating in an interview that he felt shaped by all cultures and was comfortable among them, and noted that obstinacy and tenacity, a Turkish tradition, were part of his character and beneficial to developing fuzzy logic. He described himself as "an American, mathematically oriented, electrical engineer of Iranian descent, born in Russia." He and his wife Fay had two children, Stella and Norman Zadeh, and she wrote a book, My Life and Travels with the Father of Fuzzy Logic, about their travels and experiences. Zadeh died in his home in Berkeley, California, on 6 September 2017, at the age of 96, and was buried on 29 September 2017 at the First Alley of Honors in Baku, Azerbaijan, the city of his birth. His funeral was well attended by highly respected people, and a month before his death, the University of Tehran released an erroneous report claiming his death, which it later withdrew. According to Google Scholar, as of November 2021, Zadeh's work had been cited at least 269,091 times, with his 1965 Fuzzy sets paper receiving at least 122,743 citations. In his theory of fuzzy sets, he proposed a membership function with a range from [0,1], introduced new operations for logic calculus, showed that fuzzy logic generalizes classical and Boolean logic, and proposed fuzzy numbers as a special case of fuzzy sets with corresponding rules for fuzzy arithmetic. His research significantly impacted artificial intelligence, as fuzzy sets and fuzzy logic are motivated by human cognition's comfort with vague boundaries, aligning with the Physical symbol system assumption in AI. The concept of a linguistic variable in fuzzy logic connects a predicate (e.g., "John is Bold") to linguistic values (e.g., "John is somewhat bold"), generalizing binary logic to a continuum from 0 to 1, allowing expressions like Bold(John)=0.5, and enabling the use of fuzzy sets like "somewhat bold" to describe human-like semantics, moving beyond numerical or interval descriptions. Zadeh was an active contributor to the AI community, including at the Dartmouth Workshop that coined the term "artificial intelligence," and frequently contributed to leading AI conferences such as AAAI and IJCAI, as well as AI Magazine. He is credited, along with John R. Ragazzini, with pioneering the Z-transform method in discrete-time signal processing in 1952, which is now standard in digital signal processing, digital control, and related fields. He was an editor of the International Journal of Computational Cognition. His later work included papers on computing with words and perceptions, such as "From Search Engines to Question-Answering Systems" and "Toward a Generalized Theory of Uncertainty (GTU)—An Outline." A complete list of his publications is available. Zadeh was a Fellow of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, the Association for Computing Machinery, the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence, and the International Fuzzy Systems Association, and a member of the National Academy of Engineering. He was also a member of the Academies of Science of Azerbaijan, Bulgaria, Finland, Korea, and Poland, and the International Academy of Systems Studies in Moscow. He received 24 honorary doctorates. Awards include the IEEE Education Award (1973), and in 2014, the IEEE Systems, Man, and Cybernetics Society established the "Lotfi A. Zadeh Pioneer Award," funded by a $100,000 donation from his son Norm Zadeh, to honor pioneering contributions in systems science and engineering, human-machine systems, and cybernetics, with contributions made at least 15 years prior. In February 2019, ADA University in Baku established the first "Lotfi Zadeh Scholarships" to honor undergraduate students in IT and Engineering with a 4.0 average, offering a full tuition waiver. On 4 February 2021, the IEEE Computational Intelligence Society and the International Fuzzy Systems Association celebrated the centenary of Zadeh's birth. On 30 November 2021, Google honored Zadeh with a Google Doodle, marking the day in 1964 when his seminal paper "Fuzzy sets" was submitted for publication.
